newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria police crack down on luxury car theft.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria police crack down on luxury car theft.

text.p: Bulgarian police have taken thousands of luxury new cars for checks in a crackdown on the organised trade in stolen vehicles, Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev said on Friday.

Bonev told reporters that in Sofia alone police assigned to "Operation Mosquito" had escorted 600 Mercedes, 3,000 Audis, more than 1,000 BMWs and numerous luxury four-wheel-drive vehicles to a barracks on the outskirts of Sofia for checks to be carried out.
"We are checking the cars and we work together with the tax services so that the finance minister is very grateful to me," Bonev told reporters after meeting police chiefs.
The Interior Ministry began its operation on Thursday, seizing luxury cars to check whether they were legally owned and their customs duties and taxes paid.
Car-owners must also prove they have bought their vehicles from a legitimate source and account for the money used to pay for them.
Some owners described how they had been beaten by riot police with black hoods over their faces.

Bonev said allegations of police violence were being investigated but no one had yet lodged a complaint with the Interior Ministry. One witness who described the scene to Reuters on Thursday said he was afraid to give his name.

Bulgarians typically drive Russian Ladas and the crackdown on ill-gotten wealth has been welcomed by the public, although Douma, the daily of the former ruling Socialist Party, dismissed it as a publicity stunt.
"I hope that this will not be only a single raid but a constant policy of the ministry," Georgi Nedev, 23, told Reuters. "Young people do not want to live in a mafia state."

Police say the traffic of stolen cars through Bulgaria is huge. Groups working with gangs in Western Europe alter the appearance of vehicles and forge their documents, ready for local sale or re-export to neighbouring Balkan countries and ex-Soviet republics.
"The criminal world has built up a lot of strength and has tentacles everywhere," Bonev said. "If we give in to organised crime now, there is a danger of becoming a mafia state."
Crime has flourished in the seven years since the collapse of communist rule and poorly paid policemen have been easily corrupted.

"I am not happy with the state of the ministry, and one of our management priorities is to shake police chiefs in municipalities out of their lethargy," Bonev said. "They still live as if they are (communist) militia, not police."
